claims.text: The target nanoparticles are near-equiatomic, compositionally complex, multimetal high-entropy alloys.
Increasing Co concentration enhances local bond stiffness, particularly through Co-Al interactions.
Increasing Co concentration slows lattice diffusion.
Increasing Co concentration delays surface premelting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Increasing Co concentration elevates the melting point of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Co significantly reduces the interdiffusion coefficients of the principal alloying elements, especially Al.
Increasing Co concentration induces incompressibility in Al, which contributes to sluggish lattice diffusion.
Co modifies local atomic ordering in the nanoparticles.
Greater Co concentration raises the energy barrier for atomic rearrangements at the nanoparticle surface.
Reduced interdiffusion limits the onset of surface disorder.
Limiting surface disorder produces a higher effective melting temperature.
Higher-Co nanoparticles will show a statistically significant increase in premelting-onset temperature relative to lower-Co nanoparticles.
Higher-Co nanoparticles will show a statistically significant increase in melting temperature relative to lower-Co nanoparticles.
The proposed effect should hold for compositionally complex high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles approximately 5–20 nm in size.
The magnitude of the premelting and melting shifts may depend on synthesis method, particle-size distribution, and interactions with alloying elements other than Co and Al.
A controlled comparison would vary Co concentration while holding particle-size distribution and alloy complexity constant.
Premelting onset, melting temperature, and interdiffusion rate would be measured during controlled heating under inert conditions.
Failure of higher-Co nanoparticles to show a statistically significant delay in premelting or increase in melting temperature would falsify the proposed mechanism.
